title: Cash Flow Statement
description: Class 12 Accountancy: cash flow statement (AS-3) — meaning, objectives and classification into operating, investing and financing activities, with the indirect method for operating cash flow and worked examples.

topics.title: Meaning, Objectives and Classification of Activities
topics.concept:
Profit is not the same as cash — a firm can be profitable yet short of cash (e.g. profits locked in debtors or stock). A Cash Flow Statement shows the inflows and outflows of cash and cash equivalents during a period, explaining why the cash balance changed. It is prepared as per AS-3 (Revised) and is mandatory for most companies.

Cash means cash in hand and demand deposits; cash equivalents are short-term, highly liquid investments readily convertible into known amounts of cash (e.g. treasury bills, very short-term deposits).

Its objectives are to: show the sources and uses of cash, assess the firm's ability to generate cash and pay its obligations, explain the difference between profit and cash, and help in short-term financial planning.

The statement classifies all cash flows into three activities:

ActivityIncludes
Operatingthe firm's main revenue-producing activities (cash from customers, payments to suppliers/employees)
Investingpurchase/sale of fixed assets and (non-trade) investments
Financingchanges in owners' capital and borrowings (shares, debentures, loans, dividends)

A useful rule for classifying: ask which part of the business the cash relates to. Cash from selling goods is operating; cash spent buying machinery is investing; cash raised by issuing shares is financing. (For a finance company, interest and dividends may be operating, but for a normal firm interest paid and dividends paid are financing.) Correct classification is the heart of this chapter.

examples.problem: Example 1: What does a cash flow statement show?
examples.solution:
Cash movements.

  • The inflows and outflows of cash and cash equivalents during a period.
examples.answer: The inflows and outflows of cash and cash equivalents during a period (and why the cash balance changed).

examples.problem: Example 2: Under which activity is the purchase of machinery classified?
Example 3: Under which activity is cash raised by issuing shares classified?

recap:
• Cash Flow Statement (AS-3) explains the change in cash & cash equivalents; profit ≠ cash.
  • Three activities: Operating (main business), Investing (fixed assets & investments), Financing (capital, borrowings, dividends).
  • Classify by asking which part of the business the cash relates to.

quiz.q: Purchase of a building is classified under ____ activities.
quiz.explanation: Buying fixed assets is an investing activity.

quiz.q: Issue of shares for cash is classified under ____ activities.
quiz.explanation: Raising owners' funds is a financing activity.

topics.title: Cash Flow from Operating Activities
topics.concept:
Operating activities are the firm's main revenue-producing activities. Cash flow from operations is usually found by the indirect method, which starts from net profit and adjusts it back to cash — because net profit is computed on the accrual basis and includes non-cash and non-operating items.

The steps of the indirect method:

  1. Start with Net Profit before Tax and Extraordinary items (work it up from the change in the P&L balance + provision for tax + proposed dividend + transfer to reserves).
  2. Add back non-cash and non-operating expenses — depreciation, goodwill/patents written off, interest paid, loss on sale of assets.
  3. Subtract non-operating incomes — interest/dividend received, profit on sale of assets.
  4. This gives Operating Profit before Working Capital Changes.
  5. Adjust working capital changes: add a decrease in current assets and an increase in current liabilities; subtract an increase in current assets and a decrease in current liabilities.
  6. Subtract tax paid to get Cash Flow from Operating Activities.

The logic of step 5 is intuitive: if debtors rise, sales have not yet been collected in cash, so cash is lower than profit (subtract); if creditors rise, the firm has held on to cash it owes, so cash is higher (add).

For example, net profit before tax Rs 2,00,000; add depreciation Rs 40,000 and interest Rs 10,000; less profit on sale of asset Rs 5,000 → operating profit before working capital changes Rs 2,45,000. If debtors rose Rs 30,000 (subtract) and creditors rose Rs 20,000 (add), and tax paid was Rs 35,000, then operating cash flow = 2,45,000 − 30,000 + 20,000 − 35,000 = Rs 2,00,000. This reconciliation of profit to cash is the most important computation of the chapter.

examples.problem: Example 1: Why is depreciation added back in the indirect method?
examples.solution:
Non-cash expense.

  • Depreciation reduced profit but involved no cash outflow.
  • So it is added back to convert profit to cash.
examples.answer: Because it is a non-cash expense that reduced profit without any cash outflow.

examples.problem: Example 2: An increase in debtors is added or subtracted in operating cash flow?
examples.solution:
Cash not yet received.

  • A rise in debtors means sales not yet collected → subtract.
examples.answer: Subtracted (a rise in debtors means cash is yet to be collected).

examples.problem: Example 3: An increase in creditors is added or subtracted?
examples.solution:
Cash retained.

  • A rise in creditors means cash not yet paid → add.
examples.answer: Added (a rise in creditors means cash has been retained).

recap:
• Indirect method: start with net profit before tax; add back non-cash/non-operating expenses (depreciation, interest, loss on sale); subtract non-operating incomes.
  • Then adjust working capital: + decrease in CA / increase in CL; − increase in CA / decrease in CL; finally subtract tax paid.
  • Result = Cash Flow from Operating Activities (reconciles profit to cash).

quiz.q: In the indirect method, depreciation is:
quiz.explanation: It is a non-cash expense, added back.

quiz.q: An increase in current liabilities (e.g. creditors) is:
quiz.explanation: A rise in current liabilities adds to operating cash flow.

topics.title: Cash Flow from Investing and Financing Activities
topics.concept:
After operating activities, the other two sections are more direct.

Investing activities — cash flows from buying and selling fixed assets and non-current (non-trade) investments:

  • Outflows (subtract): purchase of fixed assets, purchase of investments.
  • Inflows (add): sale of fixed assets, sale of investments, interest and dividend received.

Financing activities — cash flows from changes in the firm's capital and borrowings:

  • Inflows (add): issue of shares, issue of debentures, raising loans (and securities premium received).
  • Outflows (subtract): redemption of debentures/preference shares, repayment of loans, interest paid, dividend paid.

Finally, the three sections are combined:

Net Increase/Decrease in Cash = Operating + Investing + Financing flows

This net figure is then added to the opening cash & cash equivalents to arrive at the closing cash & cash equivalents — which must agree with the cash and bank balances in the balance sheet. That agreement is the proof that the statement is correct.

For example, if operating cash flow is +Rs 2,00,000, investing is −Rs 1,20,000 (bought machinery) and financing is +Rs 50,000 (issued shares less dividend paid), the net increase in cash = Rs 1,30,000; added to opening cash of Rs 40,000, closing cash = Rs 1,70,000. With this, you can explain exactly how a company's cash position moved over the year — the capstone of Class 12 Accountancy, and a skill prized in CUET, B.Com and CA Foundation alike.

examples.problem: Example 1: Sale of old machinery for cash is classified under which activity?
Example 2: Dividend paid by a company is classified under which activity?
Example 3: Operating +2,00,000; investing −1,50,000; financing +30,000; opening cash 50,000. Find closing cash.

recap:
• Investing: − purchase of fixed assets/investments; + sale of fixed assets/investments, interest & dividend received.
  • Financing: + issue of shares/debentures/loans; − redemption/repayment, interest paid, dividend paid.
  • Net change = Operating + Investing + Financing; opening cash + net change = closing cash (must match the balance sheet).

quiz.q: Purchase of non-current investments is classified under:
quiz.explanation: Buying investments is an investing activity.

quiz.q: Redemption of debentures is classified under:
quiz.explanation: Repaying borrowings is a financing activity.

questions.q: A cash flow statement shows the inflows and outflows of:
questions.explanation: It tracks cash and cash equivalents.

questions.q: The cash flow statement is prepared as per:
questions.explanation: AS-3 (Revised) governs the cash flow statement.

questions.q: Cash flows are classified into how many activities?
questions.explanation: Operating, investing and financing — three activities.

questions.q: Cash received from customers is an ____ activity.
questions.explanation: It relates to the main business — operating.

questions.q: Purchase of machinery is an ____ activity.
questions.explanation: Buying fixed assets is investing.

questions.q: Issue of shares for cash is a ____ activity.
questions.explanation: Raising owners' funds is financing.

questions.q: In the indirect method, operating cash flow starts from:
questions.explanation: It starts with net profit before tax and adjusts.

questions.q: Depreciation in the indirect method is:
questions.explanation: It is a non-cash expense, added back.

questions.q: An increase in debtors is ____ in operating cash flow.
questions.explanation: Cash not yet collected, so subtract.

questions.q: An increase in creditors is ____ in operating cash flow.
questions.explanation: Cash retained, so add.

questions.q: Sale of a fixed asset is an ____ activity.
questions.explanation: Selling fixed assets is investing.

questions.q: Dividend paid by a company is a ____ activity.
questions.explanation: Dividend paid is a financing outflow.

questions.q: Interest received on investments is generally an ____ activity (non-finance firm).
questions.explanation: For a normal firm it is investing.

questions.q: Net increase in cash =
questions.explanation: Sum the three activities' flows.

questions.q: Closing cash must agree with the cash and bank balances in the:
questions.explanation: Closing cash equals the balance sheet's cash & equivalents.

questions.q: Net profit before tax Rs 1,50,000; depreciation Rs 30,000; profit on sale of asset Rs 8,000. Operating profit before working-capital changes is:
questions.explanation: 1,50,000 + 30,000 (add depreciation) − 8,000 (less profit on sale) = 1,72,000.

questions.q: During the year debtors rose Rs 40,000, creditors rose Rs 25,000 and inventory fell Rs 10,000. The net working-capital adjustment to operating cash is:
questions.explanation: − 40,000 (debtors up) + 25,000 (creditors up) + 10,000 (stock down) = −5,000.

questions.q: Why does a profitable company sometimes show NEGATIVE operating cash flow?
options: Profit is locked in rising debtors/inventory, so cash hasn't been received
questions.explanation: Accrual profit can be tied up in working capital, leaving little or negative operating cash.

questions.q: A machine (book value Rs 50,000) is sold for Rs 60,000. In the cash flow statement this gives:
options: Investing inflow Rs 60,000; and Rs 10,000 profit removed from operating profit
questions.explanation: The full Rs 60,000 sale proceeds are an investing inflow; the Rs 10,000 profit is deducted in the operating section to avoid double counting.

questions.q: Operating cash flow +Rs 3,00,000; investing −Rs 2,40,000; financing −Rs 20,000; opening cash Rs 60,000. Closing cash is:
For a normal (non-finance) company, interest paid on a loan is classified as:
questions.explanation: Interest paid relates to borrowed funds, a financing activity for a non-finance firm.

questions.q: Proposed dividend of the previous year, paid this year, is shown as:
options: A financing outflow when actually paid
questions.explanation: Dividend actually paid during the year is a financing outflow.

questions.q: Which item is added back to net profit AND also shown separately as an outflow elsewhere?
options: Interest on borrowings (added back in operating, shown as financing outflow)
questions.explanation: Interest is removed from operating profit (added back) and the cash interest is shown under financing.

questions.q: Closing cash computed in the statement does NOT match the balance sheet's cash. This means:
options: An error or omission in the cash flow statement
questions.explanation: The statement's closing cash must reconcile to the balance sheet; a mismatch signals an error.

questions.q: The fundamental purpose of the cash flow statement is to:
options: Explain why cash changed and bridge the gap between profit and cash
questions.explanation: It reconciles accrual profit to actual cash and reveals how cash was generated and used.
